description: We are environmental engineering students from Ilo, Moquegua, in southern Peru. We use NASA open data and AI to detect how temperature, rainfall and soil moisture are changing across our region, from the Pacific coast to the high Andes, and what it means for local water supply.
summary: Yachachiq (Quechua for "the one who knows and teaches what they know") is a free mobile web app that turns 45 years of NASA climate data into simple, spoken advice for small farmers in Moquegua, Peru, many of whom have little formal schooling or speak Quechua or Aymara. We analyzed NASA POWER (MERRA-2) temperature and precipitation for six climate zones (1981-2025), detected trends with the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, and checked rainfall against NASA GPM IMERG satellite data analyzed in NASA Giovanni. The app answers the challenge's questions (what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant) in three simple steps: 1) Today: rain and heat or frost in the last 30 days, and how much hotter the area is than 40 years ago, with a color map of all zones; 2) Next month: a temperature forecast from a model retrained every day, the normal rain and what to prepare, with step-by-step voice guides; 3) My crops: advice for each local crop. It uses words instead of decimals, talks in Spanish, English, Quechua and Aymara, and updates itself every day. Key finding: temperature is rising 0.2-0.3 °C per decade in five of the six zones, while monthly rainfall cannot be forecast reliably, and the app says so honestly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Yachachiq (Quechua for "the one who knows and teaches what they know") is a free web app, designed for the phone, that helps a small farmer in Moquegua (southern Peru) plan the farm with 45 years of NASA data. Climate information in Peru usually comes as technical charts in written Spanish, so it does not reach many rural farmers. We turned NASA data into answers they can see and hear, in three steps: Today, Next month and My crops.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) monthly temperature and precipitation for six climate zones of Moquegua, from the coast (Ilo) to the high plateau (1981-2025). We checked rainfall against NASA GPM IMERG monthly and daily data in NASA Giovanni (time series for each zone) and removed 18 false rainfall months.

2. Trends: Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope for each zone and variable, to say what is changing, where, how much and whether the change is significant. We compared the historical average, a linear regression (month + trend + El Niño) and a Random Forest, trained on 1981-2012 and tested on 2013-2025. Random Forest overfitted and was discarded. Temperature can be forecast better than the average; monthly rain cannot, so the app only shows the normal rain for rain.

3. Step 1, Today: rain and heat (or frost in the highlands) of the last 30 days compared with the same dates of every year, and how much hotter the area is than 40 years ago, plus a map with the color of every zone.

4. Step 2, Next month: a separate, clearly labeled forecast screen with next month's temperature, the normal rain for that month, the summer outlook and "Get ready for December" tasks. Each task opens an animated step-by-step guide with voice (store water, irrigate in cool hours, clean canals, protect crops, animals and skin from heat and frost), checked against FAO, MINSA, SENAMHI and MIDAGRI.

5. Step 3, My crops: advice for seven local crops (olive, alfalfa, avocado, grape, potato, oregano, pastures).

6. It updates itself every day: the phone downloads the NASA POWER daily series, recomputes "Today" and retrains the next-month temperature model with every month up to today (we checked it against our notebook: same result within 0.1 °C). A GitHub Actions robot downloads every morning the NOAA El Niño index and NASA GPM IMERG daily rain (Earthdata Cloud) for the six zones.

7. Made for people who read little: words instead of decimals ("about double the normal rain", "a little hotter than 40 years ago"), a farmer character, Manuel, who reads everything aloud, automatic location, and Spanish, English, Quechua and Aymara with the language suggested by area (Peruvian Ministry of Culture data). A daily fact from NASA data and one piece of Andean ancestral knowledge per day.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It lets people who cannot read charts, or who do not read at all, understand long-term climate trends in their own area and act on them: save water before a dry summer, irrigate at better hours, protect crops and livestock from frost. It is free, needs no sign-up, works on a basic phone and can be replicated in any region of Peru by changing the coordinates.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, scipy, scikit-learn) for the analysis; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with animated SVG illustrations for the app; Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map; Chart.js on the technical page; GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions. Code: https://github.com/sbx-cmyk/pulso-del-agua . Technical page with all tests and sources: https://sbx-cmyk.github.io/pulso-del-agua/tecnico.html

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honesty: the app says what it knows and what it does not; daily forecasts are left to SENAMHI. Accessibility: big icons, voice, few words and local languages. Respect for local knowledge: traditional signs are shown as traditions, not as verified forecasts. AI use is declared: code, illustrations (marked "AI"), logos and voices were made with AI tools and reviewed by the team; the Quechua and Aymara texts are AI-assisted drafts that we will review with native speakers.
